“The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook.” Literature on credit channels and balance-sheet constraints supports the Fed’s response: by cutting rates to the effective lower bound and launching large purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS alongside expanded repos and swap lines, the Fed aims to compress the external finance premium and stabilize bank lending—consistent with Gertler and Gilchrist (1994), Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein (1994), and Oliner and Rudebusch (1996a), as well as evidence that bank loan supply shocks are tied to capital ratios and reserve requirements. Easing capital/liquidity buffers and reserve requirements directly targets these frictions. With market-based inflation compensation falling, the literature on deflation risks and inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson) underscores the need to anchor expectations around the 2% objective; the Fed’s aggressive, pre-emptive stance reflects lessons from the 1970s’ delayed response and the importance of maintaining credibility. Overall, the near-term macro outlook remains negative due to the pandemic shock, but the policy mix materially mitigates downside risks to credit and output.
